title: T1590 — Gather Victim Network Information
subtitle: The animation shows one full network profiling run in eight short scenes.

nodes.label: Sensitive data
nodes.tip: Sensitive data - What is at risk

steps.title: Meet the players
steps.caption: The attacker laptop sits outside. The victim company runs a firewall, a DNS server, a mail and OWA server, and a VPN portal. A SOC analyst watches from inside. Nothing has happened yet.
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: DNS questions
steps.caption: The attacker asks the victim DNS server about vpn, mail, and autodiscover names, and records every answer, including the NXDOMAIN misses. This is the first direct touch of a victim system.
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: Read scan databases
steps.caption: Instead of scanning, the attacker reads stored results from a public scan service: OWA on 443, mail on 25, the VPN portal on 443, and an old appliance banner. Someone else did the scanning long ago.
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: Banner grabbing
steps.caption: The attacker opens very short connections to ports 443 and 25, reads the service greeting, and hangs up at once. The firewall logs the blocked attempts. Short connections hide inside normal noise.
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: The map is complete
steps.caption: The attacker notes now hold domains, the address block, the doors, an old appliance version, and a vendor with remote access. The mail door is marked as the target. Every line came from public data or one small probe.

steps.caption: The SOC sees only a few small traces: DNS questions from one outside address and blocked probes at the firewall, spread over days. The research must touch the edge, so log it, baseline it, and correlate by source IP.
